newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian rate cut likely, but timing unknown.
newsitem.headline: Australian rate cut likely, but timing unknown.

text.p: A fifth cut in interest rates by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is widely expected by financial markets, but no one is quite sure when it will come.
Stagnant unemployment, falling consumer confidence and continued low inflation all add up to another rate cut, analysts said.

"The weak labour force data combined with softness in business and consumer sentiment surveys in May and June as well as declining inflationary expectations have increased the likelihood of the Reserve Bank cutting rates again," UBS
Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
Asked about the chance of another rate cut, the median forecast from 30 economists surveyed by Reuters is a 60 percent chance of another rate cut, up from 35 percent just two weeks ago.
The key factor behind the increased chance of a cut has been the fall in May employment of 40,300, with the unemployment rate rising to 8.8 percent, according to official data issued last week.

"Whilst the sharp fall does not significantly add to the economic case for a fifth easing, a labour market deterioration of that magnitude will increase the political pressure on the RBA to ease again," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.

The RBA has cut rates by 50 basis points on four occasions since last July, most recently on May 23, taking them to their current level of 5.50 percent. Each time, the weak labour market has been a key factor.

With a rate cut seen as likely, markets now have to try and work out when the cut will take place. The RBA board meets once a month, but it can change monetary policy settings on any day, a fact financial markets have become painfully aware of with the last two rate cuts catching them off guard.
Over the next two weeks there are no major data seen likely to trigger an RBA move, meaning that any move is likely to follow the July 1 RBA board meeting.

"The bias, us included, is that it is more likely that rates will go down than not, and if they didn't consider a 40,000 fall in employment to be enough to cut rates, we're not really sure what they're going to wait for now -- the next big series of data isn't now until early July," Citibank senior economist Annette Beacher said.
Even then, some see the RBA waiting until the next round of inflation and wages data is released in late July.

"There's no new information out between now and the next board meeting, in fact the critical information they're likely to be looking at really comes in late July," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell senior economist Bruce Hockman said.
In the middle of all this is a meeting of the U.S. FOMC on July 1 and 2 at which U.S. rates could rise and which analysts said could influence the timing of a local move.
U.S. and Australian official rates are level at 5.50 percent, and it is uncharted territory for Australian rates to be lower than those of the United States.

As a result, some believe that if the U.S. raises rates on July 2, the RBA may allow the market time to adjust to the new rate settings rather than cutting on the same day, although a U.S. rate hike will not prevent an opposite move at home.

"The Reserve Bank has a history of doing what it thinks is required for the domestic economy and not worrying too much about the U.S, although it does pose a particular problem at this next meeting of the Reserve Bank board," DMG's Hockman said.
The bias is towards an easing, and Hockman felt the U.S influence on it is more one of timing of the move rather than whether a cut is required.
